chapters.title: Good and Bad Strategy
chapters.sourcePressure: Apple in 1997 shows the difference between strategy and ambition: Jobs narrowed product lines, channels, manufacturing, inventory, and software work around the real obstacle instead of adding slogans or broad effort.
chapters.coreMove: Replace ambition language with a diagnosis of the governing obstacle and a coordinated set of actions that actually fit it.
chapters.commonMisread: Good strategy means having a bold vision, tighter costs, or more executive energy.

chapters.title: Discovering Power
chapters.sourcePressure: David and Goliath, Wal-Mart, and Marshall and Roche point to hidden power: change the terms of contest, find the reinforcing system, or impose asymmetric costs instead of matching the visible fight.
chapters.coreMove: Look beneath the obvious contest for the hidden asymmetry that changes what strength means.
chapters.commonMisread: Power means being bigger, louder, better funded, or more determined.

chapters.title: Bad Strategy
chapters.sourcePressure: This chapter isolates recurring failure patterns: plans that sound energetic while missing diagnosis, dodging tradeoffs, piling initiatives, or failing to use leverage already present in the situation.
chapters.coreMove: Spot when strategic language is covering an absent diagnosis and no real choice.
chapters.commonMisread: Bad strategy is merely a weak plan, poor execution, or low morale.
mustNotDriftInto: full taxonomy beyond the frozen source

chapters.title: Why So Much Bad Strategy?
chapters.sourcePressure: The source frames this as a causes chapter: institutions keep producing vague plans because ambiguity protects consensus, avoids painful choice, and lets rooms feel aligned before anything is excluded.
chapters.coreMove: Diagnose the social reward for ambiguity before accepting a plan as agreement.
chapters.commonMisread: Bad strategy persists because people are unintelligent or lazy.

chapters.title: The Kernel of Good Strategy
chapters.sourcePressure: The supported core is diagnosis, guiding policy, and coherent action: name the obstacle, choose the directional response, and align action rather than treating any one part as enough.
chapters.coreMove: Assemble diagnosis, guiding policy, and coherent action into one testable structure.
chapters.commonMisread: The kernel is a slogan, template, or three separate checklist items.

chapters.title: Sources of Power
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter asks where strategic force comes from before leverage is applied: recurring, durable conditions that change the contest rather than temporary tricks or copied surface moves.
chapters.coreMove: Separate durable sources of power from temporary surprise or copied tactics.
chapters.commonMisread: A source of power is any advantage, resource, or clever trick.
mustNotDriftInto: official enumerated lists not in source

chapters.title: Using Leverage
chapters.sourcePressure: This chapter turns discovered power into aimed force: focus effort at the pivot point where a small, concentrated action changes more than broad activity can.
chapters.coreMove: Aim force at the pivot point instead of distributing effort evenly.
chapters.commonMisread: Leverage means working harder, being efficient everywhere, or finding a shortcut.

chapters.title: Proximate Objectives
chapters.sourcePressure: Proximate objectives give concentrated force a credible next target under uncertainty: close enough to coordinate action without pretending the whole path is known.
chapters.coreMove: Translate uncertainty into a near-enough objective people can act on now.
chapters.commonMisread: A proximate objective is just a quarterly goal or easier milestone.

chapters.title: Chain-Link Systems
chapters.sourcePressure: Some systems are governed by their weakest indispensable link, so strengthening a strong link cannot compensate for a broken necessary one.
chapters.coreMove: Find the indispensable weak link that caps the whole system and repair it systemically.
chapters.commonMisread: Improve the average performance of the system and the weak part will matter less.

chapters.title: Design
chapters.sourcePressure: Strategy becomes design when choices fit and reinforce one another around structural limits rather than existing as isolated improvements.
chapters.coreMove: Arrange choices so they reinforce one another as a designed whole.
chapters.commonMisread: Design means making the plan elegant, creative, or visually polished.

chapters.title: Focus
chapters.sourcePressure: Focus decides where the designed whole will concentrate force; it is selective intensity under constraint, not universal coverage.
chapters.coreMove: Choose the few efforts that deserve concentrated force and let the rest stay secondary.
chapters.commonMisread: Focus means saying fewer things, having fewer meetings, or paying attention better.

chapters.title: Growth
chapters.sourcePressure: Growth is tested as a strategic outcome with costs and constraints, not an automatic virtue; expansion matters only when it preserves or strengthens strategic force.
chapters.coreMove: Judge growth by whether it strengthens the strategy or dissolves its focus.
chapters.commonMisread: Growth is always evidence that strategy is working.

chapters.title: Using Dynamics
chapters.sourcePressure: Movement over time creates openings and traps that static position misses; sequence, reaction, timing, and changing options matter strategically.
chapters.coreMove: Read the motion in the situation before choosing when and how to move.
chapters.commonMisread: Dynamics means moving fast or responding to change in general.

chapters.title: Inertia and Entropy
chapters.sourcePressure: Organizations resist change and decay for structural reasons; inertia is built-in drag and entropy is loss of coherence over time.
chapters.coreMove: Treat resistance and drift as structural facts to diagnose and counter, not moral failures to scold.
chapters.commonMisread: Inertia and entropy mean people do not care enough.

chapters.title: Putting It Together
chapters.sourcePressure: This synthesis chapter joins diagnosis, action, force, timing, structure, and reinforcement into integrated strategic practice rather than a recap of separate concepts.
chapters.coreMove: Link the strategy pieces into one response where each part strengthens the others.
chapters.commonMisread: Putting it together means summarizing the prior concepts in order.

chapters.title: The Science of Strategy
chapters.sourcePressure: Strategic thinking becomes rigorous when diagnosis, causality, consequence, challenge, and refinement are explicit instead of slogan-driven or formulaic.
chapters.coreMove: Make the strategic logic causal, challengeable, and refinable before trusting it.
chapters.commonMisread: The science of strategy means using a formula, model, or certainty machine.

chapters.title: Using Your Head
chapters.sourcePressure: The close shifts to disciplined thinking habits: skepticism, analogy risk, active judgment, and resistance to wishful interpretation under pressure.
chapters.coreMove: Slow the mind down enough to test easy stories, analogies, and preferred interpretations.
chapters.commonMisread: Using your head means being smarter, more rational, or more confident.
